patient_information: A 55-year-old indigenous Australian woman living in a crowded back room in a remote indigenous community in tropical northern Australia.
chief_complaint: Widespread exfoliating rash and sepsis, and she had become increasingly withdrawn and was not getting out of the house much.
history_of_present_illness: She presented with a widespread exfoliative rash involving all limbs, especially the armpits, buttocks, and thighs, with many skin flakes covering her mattress and fissures over her wrists and knees, appearing pale, clammy, and poorly responsive.
exposure_and_epidemiology: She lives in a crowded back room in a remote indigenous community where scabies is endemic, and many household members, particularly children, had multiple scabies lesions with secondary pyoderma.
vitals: Temperature 39.5°C (103.1°F), heart rate 110bpm, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, blood pressure 85 mmHg systolic to radial pulsation, and oxygen saturation 92% on room air. After IV fluids, BP rose to 95 mmHg systolic and O2 sat was 97% with oxygen by nasal prongs.
physical_exam: Widespread exfoliative rash involving all limbs, especially armpits, buttocks, and thighs, with many flakes of skin and fissures over wrists and knees; she appeared pale, clammy, and poorly responsive.
labs_and_diagnostics: Skin scrapings showed multiple scabies mites of varying maturity and eggs. Blood cultures grew S. aureus resistant to flucloxacillin and clindamycin but sensitive to gentamicin, co-trimoxazole, and doxycycline (community-acquired MRSA). A transthoracic echocardiogram showed no features of endocarditis. Repeated blood cultures 48 hours after admission were negative.
differential_diagnosis: Psoriasis, extensive tinea corporis, skin malignancies such as T-cell lymphomas mycosis fungoides and Sézary syndrome, nutritional deficiencies like pellagra, pemphigus, kava dermopathy, onchocerciasis, lepromatous leprosy, and secondary syphilis.
management_and_clinical_course: Initial management included oxygen, IV fluids (1 litre normal saline), and IV antibiotics (ceftriaxone 2g and gentamicin 320mg). She was evacuated to a regional hospital and managed in a single room with enhanced contact precautions. Treatment consisted of a five-dose course of ivermectin (200 µg/kg/dose), topical scabicide (benzyl benzoate 25%), keratolytic cream, and 2 weeks of IV vancomycin for MRSA. Family members were treated with topical permethrin 5%, and children with skin sores received intramuscular benzathine penicillin. She returned home after 3 weeks with no residual hyperkeratosis or shedding.
final_diagnosis: Crusted scabies with secondary sepsis likely from Staphylococcus aureus bacteraemia.
